We included 34 862 individuals (mean age 51·3 years) who participated in at least one resurvey and had no history of CVD at baseline. Participants were classified into intervention (n=25 497) and control (n=9365) groups based on the local government's targets for particulate matter reduction. We estimated the 10-year risk of incident CVD morbidity or mortality using a validated risk prediction model. We used a difference-in-difference model to assess the long-term association between CCAA implementation and predicted risk, with adjustments made for regional confounders and individual-level characteristics, including demographics, lifestyle factors, medical history, and indoor air pollution exposure. The relationship between changes in long-term exposure to PM 2·5 , PM 10 , and O 3 and predicted risk after CCAA implementation was analysed using a linear model. The estimated risk differences associated with air pollutant changes were estimated based on the magnitude of changes and their corresponding effect sizes. Findings After the CCAA was implemented, PM 2·5 and PM 10 concentrations declined in both groups, but O 3 concentrations increased. The intervention group showed a 3·95% (95% CI 3·18–4·72%) lower increase in predicted risk than the control group, with larger estimated differences under stricter enforcement. Between 2013 and 2021, each 10 μg/m 3 change in PM 2·5 concentration was positively associated with a 1·80 (1·34–2·27) percentage point change in predicted CVD risk, whereas each 10 μg/m 3 change in PM 10 concentration was associated with a 1·24 (0·84–1·63) percentage point change and each 10 μg/m 3 change in O 3 concentration with a 0·58 (0·33–0·83) percentage point change. Overall, the observed changes in air pollutants during the study period were associated with an average 6·6 percentage point reduction in predicted CVD risk. Interpretation The CCAA and improved air quality were associated with a slower increase in predicted CVD risk, supporting the necessity for stricter, multipollutant air quality policies to maximise public health benefits. Funding National Natural Science Foundation of China, Kadoorie Charitable Foundation, Noncommunicable Chronic Diseases-National Science and Technology Major Project, National Key R&D Program of China, Chinese Ministry of Science and Technology, and UK Wellcome Trust.

title: Impacts of climate-driven yield changes on the affordability of healthy diets: a modelling study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Food security is central to global nutrition improvement and public health goals, and healthy diets represent a higher-level aspiration beyond merely avoiding hunger. Climate change poses an increasing threat to food systems by affecting crop yields and food prices. Although climate change-driven risks to hunger have been widely studied, the extent to which climate change undermines the affordability of healthy diets while accounting for socioeconomic responses and regional inequalities remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to quantify the effects of climate change on the future affordability of healthy diets under alternative socioeconomic and climate scenarios. METHODS: We developed an integrated modelling framework that explicitly couples multimodel crop-yield projections with an integrated assessment model (Global Change Analysis Model [GCAM]). Yield responses from six global gridded crop models driven by four climate models were integrated into GCAM, allowing endogenous socioeconomic adjustments such as land-use shifts, production reallocation, and price responses to emerge under shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs). Diet affordability was then assessed using the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN's Cost and Affordability of a Healthy Diet framework across three socioeconomic-climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP3-6.0). FINDINGS: fertilisation effects are included, with the upper end of the model ensemble reaching about 1·6 billion people. In contrast, climate-induced affordability losses were found to be negligible under both a low-emissions pathway (ie, SSP1-2.6; -0·3 million) and a medium-emission pathway (SSP2-4.5; +0·2 million). Under a high-emission pathway, model-mean projections indicated that diet costs could increase by up to 12% in the most affected regions by the end of the century. Under medium emissions, cost increases were projected to remain below 4%, whereas under low emissions, affordability changes were projected to be minimum across regions (within approximately 0·5%). Substantial regional disparities emerged, with the largest and most consistent affordability losses concentrated in low-income regions that contributed least to historical greenhouse gas emissions. Under SSP3-6.0, these disparities persisted particularly in regions of Africa and Asia despite projected three-to-five-fold increases in income over the century, with climate-induced disruptions to food systems increasing the number of people unable to afford a healthy diet through mid-century. INTERPRETATION: Climate change is likely to exacerbate global nutritional inequalities by disproportionately increasing the affordability risks of healthy diets in regions that have contributed least to historical greenhouse gas emissions. Under high-warming scenarios, socioeconomic development alone is insufficient to fully offset these risks, highlighting the structural vulnerability of low-income food systems to climate-driven price shocks. These findings suggest that in the absence of targeted interventions, climate change could continue to undermine progress towards equitable and health-oriented nutrition outcomes. FUNDING: Ministry of Science and Technology of the People's Republic of China; National Natural Science Foundation of China; National Aeronautics and Space Administration Goddard Institute for Space Studies Climate Impacts Group; Future of Life Institute; and Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition.

title: Special Economic Zones, Casinos and the Threat of Zoonotic Diseases
Climate change and animal infectious diseases: a systematic review of emerging evidence
abstract: Climate change is increasingly recognised as a major driver of infectious disease dynamics, yet its impact on animal health remains understudied compared with its impact on human populations. This systematic review aimed to assess the effects of climate variability and change on the epidemiology of animal infectious diseases, focusing on measurable changes in disease incidence, prevalence, mortality, and geographical distribution. We searched PubMed and CAB Abstracts for studies published between Jan 1, 1970, and Dec 31, 2024, and identified 33 eligible studies that that assessed associations between climatic factors and observed disease outcomes in animal populations. The evidence base has grown over the past decade but remains geographically and taxonomically imbalanced. Most (24 [73%] of 33) studies reported positive associations between climatic variables and increased disease risk, expanded geographical ranges, or higher prevalence. Vector-mediated mechanisms were consistently proposed as underlying drivers (25 [76%] of 33). Domestic species were the most frequently studied hosts (18 [55%] of 33), whereas wildlife hosts were under-represented (11 [33%] of 33). Four studies (12%) included mixed host populations. 6200 studies identified by our search were excluded because they relied solely on environmental suitability indices, vector abundance models, or synthetic epidemiological outcomes, highlighting a persistent scarcity of longitudinal empirical disease data linked to long-term changes in weather and climate. Although modelling approaches are valuable for risk projection, the poor availability of longitudinal epidemiological data constrains validation and attribution. Overall, the available evidence suggests that climate variability and change are reshaping animal infectious disease epidemiology, with important implications for animal health, food security, and zoonotic risk. However, important gaps in our understanding of these dynamics remain. Bridging these gaps, strengthening climate-aware surveillance, expanding data accessibility, and integrating animal health into One Health strategies will be essential to address emerging health risks.

title: Urban green spaces: balancing benefits with risks from vector-borne diseases, pesticide exposure, and allergies
abstract: In 2021, mayors of 31 cities in the C40 Climate Leadership Group set 2030 targets to expand urban green space (UGS) and ensure that populations have access to nearby natural (green or blue) spaces. Research on C40’s 96 member cities estimated that a uniform increase of 1% in greenspace could reduce annual all-cause mortality by a median of 1·77 premature deaths per 100 000 people.1 Additionally, data from 11 534 urban areas spanning 2000–19 showed that increasing the enhanced vegetation index could lower global population-weighted warm-season mean temperatures by 0·08°C at a 10% increase, 0·14°C at 20%, or 0·19°C at 30%.

title: Future proofing food systems
abstract: This year is turning out to be yet another record breaker. Early in the year extreme rainfall and severe flooding afflicted North and southern Africa, parts of the UK, Spain and Portugal, Indonesia, Japan, and Brazil. The summer has seen national and regional heat records broken across North America, Africa, Europe, and Asia and 2026 looks certain to be one of the hottest, if not the hottest year globally on record. The record-breaking temperatures have accompanied prolonged and severe droughts in the western United States, large parts of South America, sub-Saharan Africa, much of Europe, and parts of Australia.

title: Premature mortality and economic losses attributable to landscape fire-related PM2·5 in ten countries and territories: a causal analysis
abstract: Background Landscape fire-related fine particulate matter (LF-PM 2·5 ) is associated with premature mortality. However, the mortality-related economic burden of LF-PM 2·5 remains poorly quantified. We aimed to estimate the short-term effects of LF-PM 2·5 on mortality and the associated economic losses. Methods In this causal analysis, we linked daily mortality records from 1366 communities in ten countries and territories during 2000–19 to population-weighted LF-PM 2·5 concentrations estimated from daily modelled data. Economic losses were estimated using adjusted values of a statistical life. We estimated community-specific associations using instrumental variable models and pooled them using random-effects meta-analysis. We compared instrumental variable estimates with traditional association estimates as well as corresponding estimates for non-LF-PM 2·5 . Findings We analysed 47 844 851 deaths, corresponding to mortality-related economic losses valued at US$60·6 trillion. Each 1 μg/m 3 increase in the 2-day moving average of LF-PM 2·5 was associated with a 0·60% (95% CI 0·19–1·00) increase in mortality and a 0·59% (0·21–0·97) increase in economic losses. An estimated 906 869 deaths and $994·5 billion in economic losses were attributable to LF-PM 2·5 , with attributable fractions of 1·90% for deaths and 1·64% for economic losses. Traditional association estimates were found to be lower than instrumental variable estimates by a median of 56·0% (2·2–111·3) for mortality and 62·3% (9·0–116·1) for economic losses. LF-PM 2·5 represented 19·0% of ambient PM 2·5 mass but accounted for 30·6% of PM 2·5 -attributable deaths and 27·7% of PM 2·5 -attributable economic losses. Interpretation Short-term exposure to LF-PM 2·5 was associated with substantial mortality and economic losses across diverse settings. The disproportionate contribution of LF-PM 2·5 to PM 2·5 -attributable burden, together with the larger instrumental-variable estimates, suggests that traditional assessments might understate the consequences of landscape fire smoke. Funding National Health and Medical Research Council, China Scholarship Council.

title: Deforestation and retail prices of Brazilian beef: a preregistered product-level econometric analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cattle ranching is the leading proximate driver of deforestation in Brazil. Efforts to eradicate deforestation could incur a trade-off between forest conservation and agricultural production, as conservation constrains the supply of new agricultural land and requires investments in traceability and improved agricultural production, potentially negatively affecting consumer welfare through increased retail prices. We estimated the effect of deforestation on consumer prices using supply chain data for 2980 beef products in Brazil. METHODS: We investigated the effect of deforestation on retail prices using a regression model with neighbourhood fixed effects and covariates, including sanitary inspection level, product type, distance from meatpacker to retail store, supply chain monitoring, and retail store size. The model was informed by a directed acyclic graph and the analysis plan was preregistered. FINDINGS: We found no evidence that deforestation rates in regions where beef products were sourced affected retail price (R$-1·26/kg, 95% CI -2·66 to 0·13 [US$0·26/kg, 0·515 to 0·025]). Similarly, the implementation of sustainable procurement criteria by meatpackers did not affect prices (R$-1·71/kg, -4·00 to 0·57 [US$0·33/kg, -0·78 to 0·11]). The main predictors of price were product type, sanitary inspection, and supply chain length. INTERPRETATION: Beef products with varying deforestation footprints appeared to be marketed through similar supply chains and priced similarly to consumers. This lack of transparency along the supply chain creates a market failure and weakens incentives for sustainable production. FUNDING: Norway's International Climate and Forest Initiative; Fonds de la Recherche Scientifique; European Research Council.

title: Effects of a 3-day simulated heatwave on physiological and functional outcomes in older adults in Canada: a single-site randomised crossover trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Laboratory-based heatwave simulations are a valuable tool for evaluating physiological and functional effects of heat exposure in vulnerable population groups (eg, older adults) and for testing the efficacy of personal cooling strategies. However, previous studies have been short in duration (2-9 h) and therefore have not captured the cumulative, multiday exposures characteristic of real-world heatwaves. We aimed to investigate physiological and functional outcomes in older adults exposed to a 3-day simulated heatwave. METHODS: We conducted a single-site, randomised, crossover trial at the Human and Environmental Physiology Research Unit at the University of Ottawa, ON, Canada. Participants were eligible if they lived in the Ottawa-Gatineau region, were aged 65-85 years, did not smoke, spoke English or French, and could provide informed consent. Exclusion criteria included severe physical restrictions, use of medication that made participation inadvisable, or cardiac abnormalities. Enrolled participants were exposed for 3 days (and 2 nights) to a simulated heatwave (34°C during the day and 26°C during the night with 45% relative humidity) and a thermoneutral control condition (26°C during both the day and night with 45% relative humidity) in a specialised climate chamber replicating a studio apartment. The two exposure sessions (ie, heatwave and control conditions) were separated by more than 10 days, and the order in which participants were assigned to each session was randomly allocated using a key generated in Microsoft Excel. Peak 1-h core (rectal) temperature was the primary outcome and was compared across days and conditions using linear mixed-effects models. Participants and investigators could not be masked to the exposure condition, but body temperature and heart rate data were processed by a masked analyst. All randomly assigned participants were included in the analyses; missing data were not imputed. The trial is registered with Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06633302) and is complete. FINDINGS: Between Oct 15, 2024, and Feb 19, 2025, 22 individuals were screened and 18 eligible participants were enrolled; the median age of all participants was 74 years (IQR 71-78), nine (50%) of the 18 participants were female, and nine (50%) were male. All participants completed both intervention periods. Daily peak core temperature was 0·4°C (95% CI 0·3-0·4) higher during the simulated heatwave exposure than during the control exposure (cross-day average: 37·8°C [SD 0·2] vs 37·4°C [0·2]; p<0·0001). No adverse events occurred. INTERPRETATION: Older adults (aged 65-85 years) exposed to a simulated 3-day heatwave showed persistent daytime elevations in core temperature, highlighting the importance of evidence-based cooling strategies and other interventions to minimise physiological strain during even moderate heat stress, and not just during the most extreme conditions. FUNDING: Health Canada and Canadian Institutes of Health Research.

title: International organisations agree on the importance of surveillance, but not on its definition
abstract: The global health impacts of pathogen spillovers, from outbreaks to epidemics and pandemics, have accelerated in the 20th and 21st centuries.1 In response, multilateral, global organisations, including WHO, coordinate to develop pandemic prevention and response strategies.2 Surveillance is at the core of any pandemic prevention or response approach, needed to capture pathogen emergence, monitor spread, and use mitigation strategies.3,4 However, whether key global entities share a common understanding of what and how surveillance occurs remains unclear.

title: Accounting for heterogeneity in mosquito exposure to forecast chikungunya outbreaks in Reunion Island and Paraguay: a mathematical modelling study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Heterogeneity in mosquito exposure at a fine spatial scale is well documented but often neglected in mathematical models of arbovirus transmission, particularly for real-time forecasting. We aimed to assess whether accounting for heterogeneity in mosquito exposure improves the ability of transmission models to reproduce past chikungunya outbreaks and to forecast an ongoing outbreak in real time. METHODS: We extended an existing transmission model, originally developed to forecast dengue outbreaks in Reunion Island and incorporating seasonality, to include heterogeneity in mosquito exposure. We compared this model to versions assuming homogeneous exposure, evaluating their ability to reproduce the 2005-06 Reunion Island outbreak and the 2023 Paraguay Metropolitana subregion outbreak. We then used the heterogeneity model to forecast the 2025 Reunion Island outbreak in real time. FINDINGS: Accounting for heterogeneity in mosquito exposure at a fine spatial scale was crucial to accurately reproduce Reunion Island's 2005-06 outbreak. Homogeneity models either overestimated final seroprevalence (80% vs 38% observed) or required a reduction of approximately 50% in the basic reproduction number following interventions, which is implausible. The heterogeneity level estimated from this outbreak transferred successfully to the Metropolitana outbreak, accurately forecasting epidemic trajectory and final seroprevalence (∼40% vs ∼75% for the homogeneity model). Under the same assumption, the heterogeneity model successfully forecasted the peak of the 2025 Reunion Island outbreak (∼400 emergency room visits per week) and timing (April), nearly two months ahead. A post-outbreak serosurvey indicated that the heterogeneity model underestimated final seroprevalence (46·1% vs 61·6% observed), whereas the homogeneity model overestimated final seroprevalence (78·5%), suggesting that heterogeneity in 2025 might have been lower than that in 2005-06. INTERPRETATION: These results highlight how incorporating heterogeneity in mosquito exposure can improve chikungunya outbreaks forecasting. Our approach showed strong predictive performance in settings with climatic seasonality and holds promise for forecasting future chikungunya and other arbovirus outbreaks. FUNDING: EU; Laboratoire d'Excellence Integrative Biology of Emerging Infectious Diseases programme; Agence Nationale de Recherches Sur le Sida, les Hépatites Virales et les Maladies Infectieuses Émergentes; Agence Nationale de la Recherche.

title: Navigating global health futures under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
abstract: The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) provide valuable insights to understand how future socioeconomic changes could alter the magnitude and pattern of climate-related risks across sectors, which might facilitate or hinder adaptation and mitigation responses. Many sectors have created SSP narrative extensions to specify insights for their domains. In this Viewpoint, we created health narrative extensions for the SSPs, considering socioeconomic and demographic drivers and population health and health-system drivers. The projected health-relevant trajectories diverge substantially over the course of the 21st century. The SSP3 and SSP4 narratives detail changes that could contribute considerable risks to health, whereas the SSP1 and SSP5 narratives highlight the role of effective governance and adequate resourcing in reducing climate-sensitive population health outcomes and health-system drivers. Given that climate forcing is considered exogenous to these narrative extensions, SSP5's favourable health driver paths do not account for the potential adverse impacts of this high-emissions pathway. The narratives elaborate population health drivers that can improve the policy relevance of population health and health-system risk projections associated with climate change across a range of possible pathways, and link these drivers with relevant cross-sectoral issues (eg, water and energy). Further research is required to quantify key drivers of population health and health-system risks at global to local scales.

title: Planetary Health Research Digest
abstract: Beyond other benefits, urban greening is often touted as a straightforward and effective way of improving air quality in cities. However, trees also emit biogenic volatile organic compounds (VOCs), such as isoprene, and in the presence of sunlight and nitrogen oxides (NOx), these compounds can contribute to the formation of ground-level ozone. Given that ozone pollution elevates risks of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, Xianjun He (Jinan University, China) and colleagues analyse the contributions of urban greening to ozone concentrations in Beijing, China.

title: From El Niño–Southern Oscillation warning to proportionate health action
abstract: A strong El Niño continues to intensify in 2026, requiring health authorities to prepare for changing rainfall and temperature patterns and associated health risks across affected regions.1 El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) can materially alter health burdens, but the magnitude and direction of the effects differ across ENSO locations and forms, as recent multicountry evidence on dengue illustrates.2 ENSO forecasts provide months of lead time, although forecast skill varies by lead time, season, model, and event.

title: Correction to Lancet Planet Health 2026; 10: 101416
Seven principles for a critical transdisciplinary approach to planetary health
abstract: The ecological, social, and health crises of the Anthropocene demand approaches to knowledge that confront complexity, uncertainty, and structural injustice. Transdisciplinarity is an approach that can transcend disciplinary silos by integrating academic and non-academic knowledge. Yet, action on public health, planetary health, and health inequities is often implemented in technocratic, depoliticised, and tokenistic ways. Such practices risk marginalising lived experience, reinforcing epistemic hierarchies, and overlooking structural drivers such as capitalism, colonialism, and patriarchy. Drawing on examples from the exposome, One Health, and planetary health paradigms, we argue that current applications of transdisciplinarity privilege biomedical or technical framings, underplay systemic power relations, and fail to deliver transformative impact. A critical transdisciplinary approach is needed-one that is political, reflexive, justice oriented, and grounded in collaboration with affected communities, social movements, and practitioners. It should integrate diverse knowledge systems, value experiential and Indigenous perspectives, and align research with agendas for structural change. We propose seven guiding principles. The approach should be: critical, systemic, structural, sociohistorical, democratic, timely, and transformative. Advancing planetary health equity requires more than an understanding of the systemic determinants of disease and environmental degradation-it requires dismantling the political, economic, and cultural systems that perpetuate them. A critical transdisciplinary approach that follows these principles can guide research, policy, and practice, positioning knowledge not only as a tool for explanation but also as an instrument for transformation.

title: Cause-specific hospital admissions associated with short-term PM2·5 exposure: a multicountry time-series analysis
abstract: Background Fine particulate matter (PM 2·5 ) pollution constitutes a leading global health burden. However, multicountry evidence about the impact of PM 2·5 on cause-specific hospitalisations, which are key markers of clinically substantial morbidity, is scarce. This study aimed to examine the association of short-term exposure to ambient PM 2·5 pollution with hospital admissions for specific causes across multiple countries. Methods We collected 346·5 million hospitalisation records from 949 communities across six countries and territories (Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, New Zealand, and Taiwan) between 2000 and 2019. At each location, we fitted quasi-Poisson generalised linear time-series models to estimate PM 2·5 -associated hospitalisation risks. These location-specific estimates were then pooled in a meta-analysis. We conducted stratified analyses by country, demographic factors, income, and time period. Findings Short-term PM 2·5 exposure was significantly associated with increases in all-cause and cause-specific hospitalisations, with effects persisting for up to 21 days. For all-cause admissions, each 10 μg/m 3 increase in PM 2·5 concentration was associated with an 8% higher risk of hospitalisation (relative risk [RR] 1·080; 95% CI 1·074–1·086), with substantial heterogeneity across countries and territories. Short-term PM 2·5 exposure was associated with increased hospitalisation risks across all disease categories, with the strongest associations observed for malignant neoplasms (RR 1·108, 95% CI 1·094–1·123), mental disorders (1·100, 1·085–1·114), other neoplasms (1·096, 1·078–1·114), and nervous system diseases (1·085, 1·069–1·102), all exceeding the RR for respiratory diseases (1·067, 1·060–1·074). Attenuated but significant risks were observed in 2010–19, compared with those in 2000–09, for all disease categories. Using a PM 2·5 concentration of 15 μg/m 3 according to the WHO daily guideline as reference, attributable measures estimated from the observed PM 2·5 –hospitalisation associations declined over time, with the attributable fraction decreasing from 8·9% in 2000–09 to 3·9% in 2010–19 and the cumulative attributable hospitalisation rate decreasing from 11·6 to 3·5 per 1000 population per year. Interpretation Our findings revealed that short-term PM 2·5 exposure was associated with persistent increased risks of hospitalisation across diverse settings. Reducing PM 2·5 exposure remains an important preventive measure to lower hospitalisation risk. Funding Australian Research Council and Australian National Health and Medical Research Council.

title: Early career insights on boundary crossing for planetary health and a just future
abstract: The complexity and boundary-crossing nature of planetary health challenges demand new ways of working and learning: pushing our own boundaries to better respond to crossing planetary limits.1 Integrative approaches to understanding health, including ecohealth, one health, and planetary health, recognise the interconnectedness and co-dependence of our social, ecological, animal, and planetary systems.2,3 This Comment underscores the value of strengthening collaboration between these integrative approaches.

title: The evidence gap behind the data centre boom
abstract: As data centres expand to meet the demands of AI, concerns about their effects on nearby communities and the environment are moving into public view. ABI Research projects that over 10 000 data centres will be operational worldwide by 2030. This expansion has been met with public scrutiny: on Sept 4, hundreds gathered in Edinburgh, Scotland, to protest a planned data centre in Auchtertool, Fife, which would be the second largest in the world. In a campaign led by the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, protestors called for a pause in development until the Scottish government produces analysis on the centre’s environmental impacts and clear planning criteria for what counts as a green datacentre.

title: The perceived impact of extreme weather events on care for people with HIV or tuberculosis and HIV in Zimbabwe: a survey-based multicentre cross-sectional observational study and formative evaluation
abstract: BACKGROUND: The growing threat to health systems posed by extreme weather events (EWEs) disproportionately affects people living with HIV and tuberculosis disease in high-burden, low-resource settings. In Zimbabwe, for example, the 2023-24 El Niño-induced drought intensified food insecurity and reduced access to clinics and medication for such vulnerable populations. We aimed to conduct a formative evaluation to assess the perceived impact of climate change and EWEs on HIV and tuberculosis determinants and service delivery and identify potential climate-adaptive health-service strategies. METHODS: In this survey-based multicentre cross-sectional observational study with a formative evaluation supplemented by qualitative data, we surveyed people living with HIV from Sept 19 to Dec 19, 2024, across 321 clinics in Zimbabwe to describe their perceived impact of EWEs on their health. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling. The inclusion criteria were being diagnosed with HIV, being older than 18 years, and receiving HIV care at Organization for Public Health Interventions and Development (OPHID) clinics during the study period. Individuals who were not receiving HIV care at an OPHID clinic or who were younger than 18 years were excluded. A client satisfaction survey was used to collect data from in-person surveys. The survey included questions related to the general effects of EWEs, such as drought, extreme heat, and flooding; how EWEs had affected HIV or tuberculosis care; and what, if any, services were currently available or should be made available to mitigate climate impacts on health. We also conducted six focus group discussions (FGDs; five to eight participants per group) between March 12 and May 12, 2024, across the Bulilima, Mangwe, and Matobo districts. We used a convenience sampling approach to select patients who had visited the health facility for medical check-ups, medication resupply, or viral load testing, as recorded in clinical registers and verified by clinical staff. Eligible participants for the FGDs were adults (≥18 years) with HIV, or with current or previous tuberculosis treatment, receiving care at the study facility during the recruitment period; those under 18 years or not receiving care at the facility were excluded. Participants' sex was self-reported at enrolment. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, whereas FGD data were analysed using a modified framework approach. The main outcomes were the perceived impact of climate change and EWEs on HIV and tuberculosis determinants and service delivery outcomes, as reported by affected communities, and community-prioritised mitigation strategies to feasibly address climate-sensitive determinants and barriers to care. FINDINGS: Among 1804 eligible participants approached across 15 districts, all completed the survey and were included in the analysis. Most survey participants (1363 [75·6%] of 1804 participants) reported noticing changes in climate over the past 5 years; of these 1363 participants, 900 (66·0%) were female and 1024 (75·1%) participants reported disruptions to their HIV care during the time they noticed changes in climate. Survey respondents reported that climate-related disruptions were associated with increased food insecurity (reported by 877 [85·6%] of 1024 participants) and water shortage (667 [65·1%] of 1024 participants). Qualitative analysis confirmed that the barriers to HIV and tuberculosis care from EWEs included widespread food insecurity, crop failures, and livestock deaths, with consequent effects on income leading to challenges in paying for food and transportation to clinics. Participants highlighted the need for expanded services that facilitate social and economic wellbeing, including nutrition support, water access, transportation, and income-generating activities, and decentralised models of health-care delivery. INTERPRETATION: Extreme heat and drought affect food and water security and have financial implications, creating challenges for patients to access care in Zimbabwe. Our findings underscore the urgent need for integrated, climate-adaptive strategies to maintain HIV and tuberculosis care in such climate-vulnerable regions. FUNDING: Nina Ireland Program in Lung Health.

title: Doing less for planetary health
abstract: The 2026 summer was not a normal one for Europe. Extreme heatwaves, droughts, wildfires, glacial collapse, and mudslides resulted in high numbers of climate-related injuries and deaths. Yet, at the end of the summer, people were still expected to return to work and re-boot the continent’s fossil fuel-based economy. Crowded commutes, endless to-do lists, and demands to work more—busyness and business-as-usual—continue. Our collective human hyperactivity consumes enormous amounts of resources and ceaselessly produces waste and emissions, causing pollution.

title: Payments for ecosystem services and their effects on health and wellbeing: a systematic review
authors: Luiz Gustavo Araújo da Cruz Casais e Silva
Juliana Araujo da Cruz Casais e Silva
abstract: Payments for ecosystem services, often funded through carbon offsetting, seek to improve environmental conservation and reduce poverty by paying individuals or communities for maintaining the environment. Following previous registration (PROSPERO CRD42024591264), we searched the EconLit, Medline, CAB Abstracts and Global Health (accessed via Web of Science), GreenFILE, and 3ie databases and grey literature. We systematically reviewed quantitative and qualitative studies assessing the effects of payments for ecosystem services on the health or subjective wellbeing of individuals. We assessed risk of bias using Risk of Bias tool for randomised trials 2, Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions, and Critical Appraisal Skills Programme, with certainty assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. Synthesis without meta-analysis, effect direction plots, and thematic synthesis were conducted. 19 (7·7%) of 5615 screened articles met the inclusion criteria, with very high or high risk of bias in most studies. Two randomised controlled trials, eight natural experiments, and nine qualitative studies were included. The synthesis without meta-analysis and effect direction plots indicated heterogeneous effects, with both beneficial and adverse effects across outcomes. Thematic synthesis suggested that payment for ecosystem services resources were often invested in health care. The reported benefits included perceived gains in happiness and pride linked to conservation activities. However, the participants also reported stress related to conditionalities or delayed payment. Community-level payments compared with individual-level payments appeared more conducive to equitable and positive health outcomes. The effects of payments for ecosystem services on health and subjective wellbeing were highly variable, depending on context and programme design. Available evidence remains scarce and has very low certainty; therefore, robust health evaluations are needed.

title: The Capitalocene: an emerging concept in public health in the midst of the current socioecological crisis
abstract: The acceleration of climate change and the rise of social inequalities in territories dominated by agribusiness, large-scale mining, and road and port projects demand a critical review of the conceptual frameworks used in public health. Given this scenario, the concept of Capitalocene, proposed by Jason W Moore,1 can be regarded as a useful analytical tool. This concept states that the current era of reconfiguration of the planet’s ecological dynamics is not explained by the alleged homogeneous responsibility of humanity, as the Anthropocene concept suggests, but rather by a specific mode of production: capitalism and its architecture of power.

title: “Spinning in circles”: a call for interdisciplinarity and situated data-driven research on urban vulnerability
abstract: Longstanding scholarship on climate change adaptation, impacts, and vulnerability highlights the need to situate new findings within an evolving body of theory and practice. In this context, the Comment by Hichem Achebak and colleagues1 in The Lancet Planetary Health prompts reflection on how their findings align with decades of intellectual and grounded work.

title: Climate overshoot
abstract: In the Late 1990s and early 2000s focussing on climate adaptation was seen by some in the climate change community as a potentially dangerous sliding of ambition on climate mitigation. Of course, it is possible to intellectually understand that mitigation, to reduce the degree of climate heating, and adaptation, to address unavoidable climate change impacts, are complementary objectives. However, there was a concern at the time that with limited political, financial, and cognitive capacity allocated to climate initiatives adaptation could, in practice, squeeze out mitigation policy.

title: Accounting for global carbon dioxide production from human metabolism between 1985 and 2015: a modelling study
abstract: Background Human activity is a dominant driver of global carbon emissions, yet one universal source–human metabolism–has never been quantified using free-living measurements of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) production at scale. We aimed to describe the contribution of human metabolism to global CO 2 emissions between 1985 and 2015. Methods In this modelling study, we used the largest available database of doubly labelled water (DLW) measurements from 1986 to 2019. The other data sources comprised WHO Global Health Observatory, United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, and Non-communicable Disease Risk Factor Collaboration. We first allometrically modelled human CO 2 production (kg per year) using measurements available for 4479 female and 2277 male participants from the International Atomic Energy Agency DLW database to derive predicted estimates of human CO 2 production adjusted for differences in body mass and sex. Second, by combining predicted estimates based on allometric scaling of CO 2 production for body mass with available population demographic information, generalised additive models were used to describe the 30-year progression of human body mass and per capita and global CO 2 production. We used the time-series country-specific measurements from 1985 to 2015 with population-level global human metabolic CO 2 production summarised as cumulative sum for the progression analyses. Findings Data were collected between 1986 and 2019. Mean ± SD (range) participant age was 40 ± 26 (0 to 101) and body mass was 63.3 ± 27.8 (2.4 to 101.9). 9006 measurements from 6756 participants (4479 women and 2277 men) from the DLW database were used to derive estimates of human CO 2 production adjusted for differences in body mass and sex. We observed that human metabolic CO 2 production approximately doubled over a 30-year period, from 1·18 Gt per year to 2·05 Gt per year. This increase was driven mostly by population growth (>60%) with a minor contribution from increases in body mass. Per capita sex differences equalised at the population level, and continental differences reflect population shifts rather than physiological differences, with Asia accounting for the majority of human metabolic CO 2 production among all continents. Interpretation Our findings suggest that human metabolism is a quantitatively important component of the fast carbon cycle and should be accounted for in carbon system modelling to enhance precision and fidelity. With a projected peak global population in the mid-to-late 21st century, metabolic CO 2 production will increasingly contribute to global carbon fluxes. title: Prioritising environmental determinants in health technology assessment: a framework for integrating environmental considerations into health-care decision making
abstract: Environmental determinants, such as air pollution, climate change, water quality, and waste, substantially influence population health, yet health technology assessment (HTA) rarely considers how health-care technologies affect these determinants and their downstream health consequences. In this Personal View, we propose a four-step prioritisation framework to identify the environmental determinants that should be prioritised for consideration in HTA. The framework maps causal pathways linking health-care technologies to environmental determinants across the lifecycle; assesses potential population health impacts; evaluates feasibility across five domains—strength of evidence, data availability, measurement standardisation, continuity of data collection, and alignment with existing HTA processes; and positions determinants within an impact–feasibility matrix to inform prioritisation. We demonstrate application of our framework using fine particulate matter (PM 2·5 ) associated with vaccine packaging as an illustrative worked example. By considering potential population health impact alongside feasibility for HTA, the framework can help identify the environmental determinants that warrant detailed assessment and those for which current evidence or data are insufficient to support assessment within HTA.

title: Correction to Lancet Planet Health 2026; 10: 101459
The impact of replacing dairy products with plant-based dairy alternatives on iodine and other micronutrients: a modelling study and evaluation of policy options to support population intake
abstract: BACKGROUND: Consumption of plant-based dairy alternatives (PBDAs) has increased as populations adopt more sustainable diets. However, PBDAs are often not fortified with key nutrients found in dairy products, particularly iodine. Iodine is essential for thyroid function and neurodevelopment, with increased importance during pregnancy, infancy, and adolescence. Iodine is often supplemented to cattle via feed, resulting in dairy products being a rich source. We assessed the impact of partly replacing dairy products with PBDAs on micronutrient intake and whether mandatory fortification of PBDAs or bread could mitigate potential shortfalls. METHODS: This modelling study combined UK national dietary data with market data on PBDA fortification. Dairy-product intake was partly or fully replaced with commercially-available PBDAs on a gram-for-gram basis, aligned with Net Zero and EAT-Lancet targets (20-100% replacement). Usual nutrient intakes were estimated using the National Cancer Institute method, and the effects on nutrient intake, adequacy, and risk of excess were evaluated under current and mandatory fortification scenarios. FINDINGS: Even partial replacement of dairy products with commercially-available PBDAs reduced iodine, calcium, riboflavin, and vitamin B12 intakes, particularly among young children, adolescents, and adult females. Replacement that aligned with the EAT-Lancet targets reduced iodine intake by 13-28%. Mandatory PBDA fortification prevented declines in micronutrient intake, although iodine inadequacy remained high among adolescent females (59% inadequate). Iodine-fortified bread improved iodine intake, reducing inadequacy among adolescent females to 37%. The combination of mandatory iodine fortification of both PBDAs and bread was the most effective strategy, maintaining or improving iodine adequacy across all population groups. There was no risk of excess nutrient intake. INTERPRETATION: Partial replacement of dairy products with PBDAs can reduce micronutrient intake under current market fortification practices, especially among population groups already at risk of iodine deficiency. However, fortification of PBDAs, bread, or both represents a feasible evidence-based strategy to counteract these reductions in micronutrient intakes, minimise the impact on population health, and inform national nutrition policy and fortification strategies during transitions to more sustainable diets. FUNDING: Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council FoodBioSystems.

title: Best practices in communication of environmental health risks due to localised pollution events: a mixed-methods systematic review
abstract: Localised environmental pollution can generate acute concern, particularly when the health effects are uncertain. Media coverage can amplify fear and stress, necessitating transparent risk communication. This mixed-methods systematic Review (PROSPERO registration number CRD42024568007) focuses on strategies for communicating health risks associated with local pollution. We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus, and PsycArticles on April 19, 2024, (from inception) and May 22, 2026 (Jan 1, 2000 onwards), supplemented by Google Scholar and OAIster (July 9, 2026), Global Index Medicus (July 10, 2026), and backward and forward citation tracking (July 16 and 17, 2026) all from Jan 1, 2000 onwards. Of 29 216 studies identified, 105 were eligible (61 quantitative, 30 qualitative, and 14 mixed-methods); all papers were written in English and included exposed populations. Review articles, animal studies, and in-vitro or in-silico studies were excluded. Quantitative outcomes comprised changes in knowledge, behaviour, stress, or fear, whereas qualitative studies analysed communication preferences or experiences. Study quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Qualitative data were analysed through thematic synthesis with CERQual assessment. Quantitative findings were narratively synthesised because of heterogeneity. Results were integrated using a convergent mixed-methods approach. Communities valued clear, plain-language explanations of pollutants, health effects, and exposure-reduction actions, supported by simple visuals and multiple communication channels. Interpersonal and community-embedded communication, especially from trusted local figures, enhanced understanding, reduced distress, and strengthened trust. Timely, consistent updates and transparent discussion of uncertainty were well received when delivered by trusted sources and combined with practical guidance but were less effective or potentially counterproductive when institutional trust was weak. Community collaboration improved the clarity, relevance, and acceptance of messages. Effective communication regarding local pollution depended on trust-building through open, empathic, and community-centred engagement. Clear, accessible messages from multiple media channels, supported by interpersonal dialogue, helped communities to understand risks without generating disproportionate worry.
